manifest_rows.title: Sparse-gap truth causes empirical-Bayes credible-set undercoverage
A sparse-gap truth lies in a hyperrectangle but is undercovered

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, a sequence
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, a truth
$\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, and $0<\alpha<\infty$ in the
procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]]. Put
$r=1+2\alpha$. Then the product prior is supported on $\ell^2$, and its
posterior kernel under the prior-predictive law $Q_{n,\alpha}$ is the product
of the coordinate laws
$$ N\!\left( \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2}, \frac{1}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right),\qquad i\ge1, $$
For $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost every observation $x$, this same kernel is
supported on $\ell^2$, and its posterior mean belongs to $\ell^2$.

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and
$$ \log\frac{dQ_{n,\alpha}}{dQ_{n,0}}(x) =-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^r}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right] =\ell_n(\alpha;x). $$
The density identity and absolute convergence hold $Q_{n,0}$-almost surely.
The same displayed score series also converges absolutely
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$ \Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}. $$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The recursion gives $N_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}^2N_j$. The preceding last gap endpoint satisfies $\rho_{j-1}N_{j-1}\le N_j/(2\rho_j)<N_j$, while the next first gap begins at $N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}N_j>2N_j$. Thus no other zero gap intersects $N_j<i\le2N_j$, where $\theta_{0,i}^2=Mi^{-1-2\beta}$. Every squared coordinate is zero or $Mi^{-1-2\beta}$, so $\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2\le M(1+(2\beta)^{-1})<\infty$ and [F3] holds. Finally $1<N_1=2^{1/s}<2=\rho_1$, so the first gap contains coordinate $1$.

Put $\delta_j=s\log\rho_j/(4\log n_j)$, $a_j=\beta+\delta_j$, $t_j=s+2\delta_j$ and $d=1+2p$. Iterating the growth bound gives $\log n_j\ge\log2+s(\log2)(j^2+2j-3)$ for $j\ge2$, hence $\delta_j\to0$. Consequently, eventually $0<\delta_j\le1/4$, $a_j<A$, $N_j/\rho_j\ge2$ and $N_j\ge2$. Restrict to these indices and put $T=s+1/2$, so $s<t_j\le T$ and $n_j^{\delta_j}=\rho_j^{s/4}$.

For $x\ge2$ and $q\ge2$, split the integers $i>x$ into intervals $(2^l x,2^{l+1}x]$. Each contains at most $3\cdot2^l x$ integers, and $\log i\le(l+2)\log x$. Hence $\sum_{i>x}i^{-q}\log i\le3x^{1-q}\log x\sum_{l\ge0}(l+2)2^{-l(q-1)}\le18x^{1-q}\log x$, because $\sum_{l\ge0}(l+2)2^{-l}=6$.

Set $n=n_j$ and first take $0\le\alpha\le\beta$. Write $t=1+2\alpha+2p$, $K=n^{1/t}$ and $q=2+2\alpha+4p+2\beta\ge2$. In [F2], use the denominator bounds $(i^t+n)^2\ge n^2$ for $i\le K$ and $(i^t+n)^2\ge i^{2t}$ for $i>K$, together with $\theta_{0,i}^2\le Mi^{-1-2\beta}$. The first part of $h_n(\alpha)$ is at most $M$, since $i^{2\alpha-2\beta}\le1$ and $\sum_{i\le K}\log i\le K\log K$. By step 2.1 the tail is at most $18Mn^2K^{-q}=18MK^{2\alpha-2\beta}\le18M$. Thus $h_n(\alpha)\le19M$ throughout $[0,\beta]$.

Now take $\beta<\alpha\le a_j$, and write $\delta=\alpha-\beta$, $t=s+2\delta$, $K=n^{1/t}$, $N=N_j$ and $\rho=\rho_j$. The zero gaps split $h_n$ into three nonnegative parts, over $i\le N/\rho$, $N<i\le2N$ and $i>\rho N$. Bounding the denominator by $n^2$, the first part satisfies $H_1\le M(\log N/\log K)(N/\rho)^{1+2\delta}/K$. Here $\log N/\log K=t/s\le T/s$ and $N^{1+2\delta}/K=n^{2\delta(t+1)/(st)}\le\rho^{(s+1)/(2s)}$, using $\delta\le\delta_j$ and $(t+1)/t\le(s+1)/s$. Therefore $H_1\le M(T/s)\rho^{-(s-1)/(2s)}$.

For the middle part use $(i^t+n)^2\ge i^{2t}$, $\log i\le\log(2N)$ and at most $2N$ indices, obtaining $H_2\le2M(\log(2N)/\log K)n^2N^{1-2s-2\delta}/K$. Since $N\ge2$, the logarithm ratio is at most $2T/s$. Also $n^2N^{1-2s-2\delta}/K=n^{-2\delta(t-1)/(st)}\le1$. Consequently $H_2\le4MT/s$.

For the last part set $q=2s+2\delta\ge2$ and apply step 2.1 at $x=\rho N$. This gives $H_3\le18M(\log(\rho N)/\log K)n^2(\rho N)^{1-q}/K$. Because $\log\rho/\log N=4\delta_j\le1$, the logarithm ratio is at most $2T/s$. Furthermore $n^2N^{1-q}/K=n^{-2\delta(t-1)/(st)}\le1$ and $\rho^{1-q}\le\rho^{1-2s}$. Thus $H_3\le36M(T/s)\rho^{1-2s}$. Combining these estimates yields $\sup_{0\le\alpha\le a_j}h_n(\alpha)\le\max(19,41T/s)M\le62M\le(32C^8)^{-1}<\tau$, since $s>1$. Hence $\underline\alpha_{n_j}\ge a_j$, and [F2] gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}(E_j)\to1$ for $E_j=\{\widehat\alpha_{n_j}\ge a_j\}$.

For fixed $\alpha$ write $B_i(\alpha)=i^{1+2\alpha}\theta_{0,i}/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$ and $W_i(\alpha)=\sqrt n\kappa_i Z_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$, so the posterior-mean error is $-B(\alpha)+W(\alpha)$. If $\alpha\ge a_j>\beta$ and $N_j<i\le2N_j$, then $i^{1+2\alpha+2p}\ge N_j^s=n$ and $n\kappa_i^2/i^{1+2\alpha}\le C^2$. There are at least $N_j/2$ integers in this block, each with squared truth at least $M(2N_j)^{-1-2\beta}$. Therefore, uniformly for $\alpha\ge a_j$, $\|B(\alpha)\|^2\ge b^2MN_j^{-2\beta}$, where $b=2^{-1-\beta}/(1+C^2)>0$.

Set $R_j=n_j^{-a_j/t_j}$ and $D=C^2(2+2^{2\beta+1/2}/(2\beta))$. At $\alpha=a_j$, put $K=n_j^{1/t_j}\ge2$. Since $v_i(a_j)\le C^2i^{2p}/(i^{t_j}+n_j)$, summing over $i\le K$ gives at most $2C^2K^{-2a_j}$. The tail is at most $\sum_{i>K}i^{-1-2a_j}\le\lfloor K\rfloor^{-2a_j}/(2a_j)\le2^{2\beta+1/2}K^{-2a_j}/(2\beta)$. Thus $V_j=\sum_i v_i(a_j)\le DR_j^2$. Each variance decreases in $\alpha$, so [F4] bounds the posterior expected squared centered norm by $V_j$ whenever $\alpha\ge a_j$. For a nonnegative random variable $Y$, integrating $u\mathbf1_{\{Y>u\}}\le Y$ gives $uP(Y>u)\le EY$. Apply this with $u=V_j/\gamma$ to bound the posterior norm quantile: $\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}r_{n_j,\gamma}(\alpha)\le\sqrt{D/\gamma}\,R_j$.

For every realization of the normal coordinates, $|W_i(\alpha)|\le|W_i(a_j)|$ whenever $\alpha\ge a_j$. Hence $\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}\|W(\alpha)\|\le\|W(a_j)\|$. By [F4], $E\|W(a_j)\|^2=\sum_i n_j\kappa_i^2/(i^{1+2a_j}+n_j\kappa_i^2)^2\le V_j\le DR_j^2$. The elementary probability bound proved in step 3.2 therefore gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}\|W(\alpha)\|>b\sqrt M N_j^{-\beta}/2\}\le4DR_j^2/(b^2MN_j^{-2\beta})$. These bounds also show almost sure square-summability simultaneously for every $\alpha\ge a_j$.

Subtracting exponents and using $n_j^{\delta_j}=\rho_j^{s/4}$ gives $R_j/N_j^{-\beta}=\rho_j^{-d/(4t_j)}$. Put $e=d/(4(s+1))$ and $\eta=d/(8(s+1)(s+1/2))>0$. Since $t_j\le T=s+1/2$, one has $d/(4t_j)-e\ge\eta$. The inflation assumption and step 3.2 imply $\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}L_{n_j}r_{n_j,\gamma}(\alpha)/(\sqrt M N_j^{-\beta})\le K_L\sqrt{D/\gamma}\,\rho_j^{-\eta}\to0$. Step 3.3's probability bound is at most $(4D/(b^2M))\rho_j^{-d/(2T)}\to0$.

On $E_j$ the selected regularity is positive and at least $a_j$. Coverage then implies $\|B(\widehat\alpha_{n_j})\|\le L_{n_j}r_{n_j,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_{n_j})+\|W(\widehat\alpha_{n_j})\|$. The left side is at least $b\sqrt M N_j^{-\beta}$ by step 3.1; the first term on the right is eventually strictly below half that amount by step 4.1, while the second exceeds the same half-threshold with probability tending to zero. Consequently coverage is at most $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}(E_j^c)+o(1)\to0$. This fixed truth in $\Theta_\beta(M)$ refutes the proposed uniform nonvanishing coverage.

boundaries.reason: One fixed infinite truth; no empty family is constructed.
No unit endpoint is asserted; gamma lies strictly between zero and one.

boundaries.evidence: The initial gap gives theta_{0,1}=0; all gaps are permitted zero coordinates, and the proof uses positive selected alpha on its high-probability event.
For large j the retained N_j<i<=2N_j block has at least N_j/2 positive coordinates.
A>beta ensures a_j<A eventually because delta_j tends to zero; M<=1/(1984 C^8), beta>0 and gamma in (0,1) are explicit. The finitely many n_j<3 are ignored asymptotically.
The truth and sample-size recursion are explicit. AC is inherited only from the stated probability model.

citations.quote:
Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$ \Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}. $$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Use [[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]], assume AC,
and fix $\beta>0$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and a finite
$A>\beta$. Run the procedure with the fixed cap $A_n=A$ and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Choose
$0<M\le(1984C^8)^{-1}$. Put $s=1+2\beta+2p$, $\rho_j=2^j$,
$n_1=2$, and
$$ n_{j+1}=\left\lceil(2\rho_{j+1}^2)^s n_j\right\rceil,\qquad N_j=n_j^{1/s}. $$
Define the fixed nonnegative truth by
$$ \theta_{0,i}^2=\begin{cases}0,&N_j/\rho_j<i\le N_j\text{ for some }j,\\0,&2N_j<i\le\rho_jN_j\text{ for some }j,\\Mi^{-1-2\beta},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$
Then $\theta_{0,1}=0$ and $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$. For every
deterministic nonnegative inflation sequence satisfying
$$ L_{n_j}\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)} $$
eventually for some finite $K_L$, one has
$$ P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L_{n_j})\}\longrightarrow0. $$
The finitely many indices with $n_j<3$ are irrelevant. In particular,
for every $\beta>0$ this gives a counterexample for any fixed cap
$A>\beta$, including constant inflation factors.

derivations.claim: The growth condition implies $N_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}^2N_j$, so $N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}N_j\ge2\rho_jN_j$. Each next first gap therefore begins beyond the preceding second gap; the two gaps with the same index are disjoint because the first ends at $N_j$ and the second begins strictly after $2N_j$. Every coordinate is zero or has squared value $Mi^{-1-2\beta}$. Hence $\sup_i i^{1+2\beta}\theta_{0,i}^2\le M$, and $\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2\le M\left(1+\int_1^\infty x^{-1-2\beta}\,dx\right)<\infty$. Thus [F1] holds.
Since $N_1=2^{1/s}$ with $s>1$, $N_1/\rho_1<1<N_1$. Therefore coordinate $1$ lies in the first zero gap and $\theta_{0,1}=0$.
The construction and its cap, credibility level and small-$M$ assumptions match [F2]. Thus the claimed vanishing coverage follows from [F2], while step 1.1 gives hyperrectangle membership.
